title: Central Limit Theorem for Dependent Random Variables
description: Formalizes the CLT beyond i.i.d. sequences to dependent random variables via two generalizations: the Martingale CLT (McLeish 1974) for martingale difference arrays with Lindeberg condition, and the α-mixing CLT (Ibragimov 1962) for stationary mixing sequences. Proves Lyapunov implies Lindeberg, i.i.d. variance convergence, and classical CLT recovery. 19 theorems, 1 axiom, 3 sorries.

title: Categorical Structure of Distributions Under Convolution
description: Formalizes the commutative monoid structure of probability distributions under convolution, with the CLT interpreted as convergence to the Gaussian fixed point. Includes Cramér's indecomposability theorem and domain of attraction formalization.

title: Free CLT: Topological Perspective in Non-Commutative Probability
description: Formalizes Voiculescu's Free Central Limit Theorem, showing that the semicircle distribution plays exactly the role of the Gaussian in non-commutative (free) probability: it is the unique fixed point and global attractor of the free renormalization flow. Includes the CLTStructure abstraction capturing the universal pattern across all five independence types.

title: Ceva's Theorem
description: Ceva's Theorem (Wiedijk #61): the algebraic equivalence that the Ceva product (AF/FB)(BD/DC)(CE/EA) = 1 iff the parameter condition def = (1-d)(1-e)(1-f) holds, proved from scratch with field_simp and linarith. The geometric interpretation (product = 1 ↔ cevians concurrent) is described in commentary but the proof is purely algebraic.

title: Ceva's Theorem: Geometric Proof via Affine Coordinates
description: Formalizes Ceva's theorem geometrically in ℝ² using affine coordinates, proving that cevians AD, BE, CF are concurrent iff d·e·f = (1-d)·(1-e)·(1-f). Extends to general triangles via affine invariance and proves medians and angle bisectors are concurrent. Includes Routh's theorem: the 1/3 parameter gives 1/7 area ratio. 39 theorems, 0 axioms.

title: Ceva's Theorem: Non-Euclidean Geometries, Menelaus Duality, and Gauss-Bonnet
description: Extension of Ceva's theorem to non-Euclidean geometries: spherical Ceva (using sin-ratios) and hyperbolic Ceva (using sinh-ratios). Includes Menelaus duality (signed product = -1 for collinear transversals), spherical excess, hyperbolic defect, and the Gauss-Bonnet formula connecting angle sums to curvature and area.

title: Ceva's Theorem: Spherical Ceva via Unit Vectors and Weight Balance
description: The spherical Ceva theorem expressed concretely using unit vectors in an inner product space. Cevian points on arcs are defined by weight parameters (α, β) via normalization of α·B + β·C. The key results: sin(BD)/sin(DC) = β/α for a single cevian, the triple product of sin-ratios equals the weight-product ratio, and the spherical Ceva concurrency condition reduces to α_D·α_E·α_F = β_D·β_E·β_F.

title: Hyperbolic Ceva's Theorem via Weight Parameters
description: Extends the weight-parameter framework for Ceva's theorem from spherical to hyperbolic geometry (hyperboloid model). Shows the same algebraic concurrency criterion — αD·αE·αF = βD·βE·βF — holds via sinh distance ratios in hyperbolic space, demonstrating the universality of the weight-parameter approach across all constant-curvature geometries. 13 theorems, 0 axioms.

title: Ceva's Theorem: Geometric Interpretation of Weight Parameters
description: Formal proof of the geometric meaning of weight parameters in Ceva's theorem: the weight pair (α, β) encoding where a cevian point D divides side BC, with ratio BD/DC = β/α. Proves 18 theorems (0 sorries, 0 axioms) covering division ratios, midpoint characterization, centroid/incenter weight conditions, and the closer-to-B criterion.

title: Ceva's Theorem for Spherical Polygons
description: Generalization of the spherical Ceva theorem from triangles to convex n-gons. For a spherical polygon P₁...Pₙ with cevian points Qᵢ on arc PᵢPᵢ₊₁ defined by weight parameters (αᵢ, βᵢ), the concurrency condition is ∏ αᵢ = ∏ βᵢ. Includes triangle/quadrilateral specializations, equal-weight (medial) case, Ceva-Menelaus duality for polygons, and scaling invariance.

title: Ceva's Theorem via Mass Point Geometry
description: Mass point geometry provides a constructive algebraic certificate for concurrent cevians: assign positive masses mA, mB, mC to vertices, and the induced ratios automatically satisfy d·e·f = (1-d)·(1-e)·(1-f). The converse is constructive: any Ceva configuration admits an explicit mass assignment.

title: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Constructive)
description: For pairwise coprime moduli, there exists a unique solution to any system of congruences. Includes the classic Sunzi problem: find n where n = 2 (mod 3), n = 3 (mod 5), n = 2 (mod 7). Answer: 23.

title: CRT Open Question: Efficient RNS Bases for Computer Arithmetic
description: Formalizes Residue Number Systems (RNS) for parallel arithmetic: definitions, concrete bases (primes, Mersenne numbers), dynamic range bounds, and correctness of RNS addition/multiplication.

title: CRT for Arbitrary-Length Moduli Lists
description: Generalizes the Chinese Remainder Theorem from fixed-size systems (2, 3, 4 moduli) to arbitrary-length lists via induction. Proves existence and uniqueness for any pairwise coprime list of moduli, with concrete examples including the Sunzi problem and a six-prime system.

title: Non-Coprime CRT for Arbitrary Lists
description: Generalizes the non-coprime Chinese Remainder Theorem to arbitrary-length systems over Euclidean domains. Proves that a system of congruences with arbitrary moduli is solvable iff all pairs satisfy the GCD compatibility condition, with solutions unique modulo the LCM of all moduli.

title: Minimal Non-Negative CRT Solution
description: For any system of congruences with pairwise coprime positive moduli, there exists a unique solution in [0, M) where M is the product of all moduli. This canonical minimal representative is obtained by reducing any solution modulo M.

title: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Non-Coprime Moduli)
description: Generalizes the Chinese Remainder Theorem to arbitrary moduli: the system x = a (mod m), x = b (mod n) is solvable iff gcd(m,n) | (a-b), with solutions unique modulo lcm(m,n).

title: CRT Computational Efficiency for Non-Coprime Moduli
description: Can the non-coprime CRT construction be made computationally efficient for large moduli? YES — three complementary improvements: (1) Solutions canonicalize to [0, lcm(m,n)) saving gcd(m,n) bits vs the naive product bound; (2) The Bézout step operates on the smaller coprime pair m/g, n/g; (3) Garner's 1959 mixed-radix decomposition bounds all arithmetic by max(m,n) per step. Together these make non-coprime CRT practical for cryptographic and computer arithmetic applications.

title: Non-Coprime CRT for Euclidean Domains and Polynomial Rings
description: Extends the non-coprime Chinese Remainder Theorem to Euclidean domains (necessity, sufficiency, uniqueness via Bézout), polynomial rings (Lagrange interpolation as CRT specialization), and PIDs via ideal theory. Proves the element-level coprimality ↔ ideal-level coprimality bridge, and gives a unified non-coprime CRT for all PIDs. 55 theorems, 0 axioms.

title: Chinese Remainder Theorem for Three Non-Coprime Moduli
description: Extends the non-coprime CRT from 2 to 3 moduli in any Euclidean domain: the system m₁∣(x-a₁), m₂∣(x-a₂), m₃∣(x-a₃) has a solution iff gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)∣(aᵢ-aⱼ) for all pairs. Proves necessity (inherited), sufficiency via iterated 2-moduli reduction, and solution uniqueness modulo lcm(m₁,lcm(m₂,m₃)). 7 theorems, 0 axioms.

title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem and CRT Lattice Connections
description: Dirichlet's approximation theorem (1842): for any real α and N ≥ 1, there exist p, q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N and |qα - p| < 1/N. Proved via pigeonhole principle on fractional part binning. Includes mediant/Stern-Brocot property, lattice point theorem, golden ratio identities, and CRT non-coprime solvability examples connecting Diophantine approximation to lattice geometry.

title: Collatz Conjecture for Structured Values
description: The Collatz sequence reaches 1 for powers of 2 and numbers of the form 2^k * m where m reaches 1. Verified cases include 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 27 (which takes 111 steps).

title: Collatz Cycles: Non-Existence of Small Cycles
description: Proves structural constraints on hypothetical Collatz cycles: no fixed points, no 2-cycles, the unique cycle through 1 is {1,4,2} with period 3, and derives algebraic bounds on cycle length from the 2^M > 3^j constraint. All n ≤ 20 verified to reach 1.

title: Extending Collatz k-Cycle Exclusion via Case Analysis
description: Addresses OQ-01 of the Collatz cycle non-existence problem: can parity case analysis be extended to rule out k-cycles for small k ≥ 4? Proves the j=1 algebraic uniqueness theorem (3n+1 = 2^M·n forces n=1, M=2), extends the halving constraint bounds to j=5..8 odd steps, and establishes minimum cycle lengths. Axiomatizes the Eliahou (1993) bound: any non-trivial cycle has period > 17 billion.

title: Growth Rate of Average Collatz Stopping Time
description: Formalizes the average Collatz stopping time S(N) and asks whether S(N) ~ c·log N. Defines stopping time via Nat.find, heuristic constant 1/log₂(4/3), and states the asymptotic growth question. Axiomatizes Terras density result.

title: Formula for the Number of Combinations
description: The number of ways to choose k elements from a set of n elements is C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!). This fundamental formula in combinatorics counts the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set.

title: Extended Binomial Coefficient Identities
description: Formalizes key binomial coefficient identities extending the basic combinations formula: Vandermonde's identity C(m+n,r) = Σ C(m,k)·C(n,r-k), the Hockey Stick identity Σᵢ C(i+r,r) = C(n+r+1,r+1), the double-counting product identity C(n,k)·C(k,j) = C(n,j)·C(n-j,k-j), row sums, bounds C(n,k) ≤ 2ⁿ and C(2n,n) ≤ 4ⁿ, and Fibonacci diagonal sums. 8 theorems, 0 axioms.

title: Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis
description: The Continuum Hypothesis is independent of ZFC set theory. Godel showed CH is consistent with ZFC; Cohen showed not-CH is also consistent.

title: Should We Adopt Axioms That Decide CH?
description: The Continuum Hypothesis is independent of ZFC, raising a natural question: should we extend our axiom system to settle it? This exploration formalizes the CH axiom landscape — V=L (implies CH) vs forcing axioms like PFA (implies ¬CH) — and reveals a key asymmetry: CH-deciding axioms are incompatible with large cardinals, while ¬CH-deciding axioms are not.

title: What Is the "True" Size of the Continuum?
description: ZFC constrains 2^aleph_0 to be a regular uncountable cardinal (Cantor + Konig), and Easton showed any such cardinal is achievable. This formalization maps the complete spectrum of possible values, introduces cardinal characteristics (bounding and dominating numbers), and compares three scenarios: CH (2^aleph_0 = aleph_1), PFA (2^aleph_0 = aleph_2), and exotic models (2^aleph_0 > aleph_2).

title: Cramer's Rule
description: For Ax = b with det(A) ≠ 0, xᵢ = det(Aᵢ)/det(A) where Aᵢ has column i replaced by b.

title: Cayley-Hamilton as a Corollary of Cramer's Rule
description: A formal proof that the Cayley-Hamilton theorem — every matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial — follows as a direct corollary of the adjugate identity at the heart of Cramer's Rule: A * adj(A) = det(A) * I.

title: Cramer's Rule: Connection to LU Decomposition
description: Formalizes the algebraic connection between Cramer's Rule and LU decomposition. Proves the LU determinant formula det(LU) = (∏ L_ii) × (∏ U_ii), the inverse formula (LU)⁻¹ = U⁻¹L⁻¹, and the solution equivalence between forward/back substitution and Cramer's cofactor formula.

title: Quasideterminant Theory: Non-Commutative Analogue of Determinants
description: Complete quasideterminant theory for 2×2 matrices over division rings. Defines all four quasideterminants (Gelfand-Retakh), proves commutative reduction to classical determinants, alternate pivoting for non-commutative Cramer's rule, Schur complement matrix inversion, row/column scaling identities, and special cases for triangular matrices.

title: Complexity Analysis: Cramer's Rule O(n!) vs Gaussian Elimination O(n³)
description: Formalizes the computational complexity comparison between Cramer's Rule and Gaussian elimination. Defines operation counts for both algorithms, proves n! ≥ n³ for n ≥ 6 by induction, and computes exact operation counts for small systems (n = 1,2,3,4). Cramer's Rule uses (n+1)·detOps(n) + n operations via the Leibniz formula, while Gaussian elimination uses O(n³).

title: Newton-Girard Identities for Matrix Characteristic Polynomials
description: Formalizes Newton's identities connecting power sums pₖ(M) = tr(Mᵏ) to the characteristic polynomial coefficients cₖ of an n×n matrix M. Proves the k=1 identity (tr(M) = -cₙ₋₁) from Mathlib's trace_eq_neg_charpoly_coeff, the k=2 and k=3 recurrences via Newton's small-k axiom, and the large-k recurrence (k ≥ n) from Cayley-Hamilton. Establishes tr(M²) = tr(M)² − 2·det(M) for 2×2 matrices and det(M) = (tr(M)² − tr(M²))/2 over fields. Completes the fourth open question of the Cramer's Rule chain.

title: Complexity Analysis: Cramer's Rule vs Gaussian Elimination
description: A formal proof that Gaussian elimination (O(n³) multiplications) is strictly more efficient than Cramer's rule ((n+1)·n·n! multiplications) for solving n×n linear systems, with the gap growing super-polynomially: for any constant K, Gaussian is eventually K-times faster.

title: Non-Commutative Cramer's Rule via Quasideterminants
description: Extends Cramer's Rule to division rings using the Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminant. For 2×2 systems Ax = b, the solution x₀ = |A|₀₀⁻¹·(b₀ - a₀₁·a₁₁⁻¹·b₁) is proved correct, unique, and shown to reduce to classical Cramer's Rule when D is commutative.

title: Cramer's Rule OQ-04: Adjugate as Generalized Inverse
description: Formalizes the adjugate matrix as a generalized inverse extending Cramer's rule to singular matrices. Proves the fundamental identities A * adj(A) = det(A) * I and adj(A) * A = det(A) * I, the 1-reflexive property A * adj(A) * A = det(A) * A, and Cramer's solution formula for non-singular systems. Proves what adj(A)*b computes in the singular case. 11 theorems, 0 definitions, 0 axioms.

title: Irrationality of ∛2
description: Proves that the cube root of 2 is irrational using Mathlib's irrational_nrt_of_notint_nrt. The proof establishes that 2 is not a perfect cube (1³ = 1 < 2 < 8 = 2³, so no integer satisfies n³ = 2), hence cbrt2 = 2^(1/3) is not an integer, hence irrational. Also provides the alternative form irrational_two_pow_one_third. 5 theorems, 1 definition, 0 axioms.

title: Irrationality of ∛3
description: Proves that the cube root of 3 is irrational using Mathlib's irrational_nrt_of_notint_nrt. Establishes that 3 is not a perfect cube (1³ = 1 < 3 < 8 = 2³), hence cbrt3 = 3^(1/3) is not an integer, hence irrational. Mirrors the proof structure of CubeRoot2Irrational. 5 theorems, 1 definition, 0 axioms.

title: De Moivre's Theorem
description: (cos θ + i sin θ)^n = cos(nθ) + i sin(nθ). Connects powers of complex numbers to multiple angle formulas.

title: Explicit Multiple Angle Formulas from De Moivre's Theorem
description: A complete formalization of the explicit extraction of cos(nθ) and sin(nθ) as polynomial expressions in cos(θ) and sin(θ), obtained by comparing real and imaginary parts of (cos θ + i sin θ)^n. The key result is that cos(nθ) = T_n(cos θ) and sin((n+1)θ) = U_n(cos θ)·sin θ, where T_n and U_n are Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kind.

title: Chebyshev Polynomial Properties via De Moivre's Theorem
description: A formalization of Chebyshev polynomial identities derived from De Moivre's theorem, proved for cos θ values via Mathlib's T_real_cos: the composition identity T_m(T_n(cos θ)) = T_{mn}(cos θ), the product-to-sum formula, parity relations, special values T_n(±1) and T_n(0), and the roots T_n(cos((2k+1)π/(2n))) = 0. All 16 theorems with 0 sorries.

title: De Moivre OQ-03: Fractional Exponents and Root Extraction
description: Extends De Moivre's theorem to fractional exponents z^(p/q), proving root enumeration, distinctness, and principal value consistency via Mathlib's cpow.

title: De Moivre Extension to Irrational Exponents
description: Extends De Moivre's theorem to real exponents via Complex.cpow. Proves the real-exponent formula on the principal branch, constructs rational multi-valued roots, and states Weyl equidistribution (axiom). Note: irrational single-valuedness theorem is a True stub (placeholder).

title: Denumerability of the Rationals
description: Cantor's proof that the rational numbers are countable: despite being dense in the reals, there exists a bijection between the natural numbers and the rationals. Wiedijk #3. Fully proved in Lean 4 using Mathlib's Denumerable typeclass.

title: Cantor's Characterization of ℚ as the Unique Countable Dense Linear Order
description: Derived from Mathlib's Order.iso_of_countable_dense: ℚ is (up to order-isomorphism) the unique countable dense linear order without endpoints. Provides bridge formalization showing ℚ satisfies the CDLO axioms, plus independent embedding results (ℤ ↪o ℚ, Fin n ↪o ℚ). Core Cantor characterization via Mathlib's back-and-forth implementation. 18 theorems, 0 axioms.

title: Stern-Brocot Tree Encoding of Rationals
description: Formalizes the Stern-Brocot tree as a state machine and proves coprimality, positivity, ordering, and injectivity — all driven by a single determinant invariant. Known to list every positive rational exactly once in lowest terms (surjectivity is future work; injectivity and coprimality proved here).

title: Constructive Denumerability of Algebraic Numbers
description: Constructive proof that the algebraic numbers are countable, avoiding the full axiom of choice. Uses polynomial countability and FTA for finite roots.

title: The Derangements Formula
description: Pedagogical presentation of Mathlib's derangement theory (Wiedijk #88): named wrappers for the recurrence $D(n+2)=(n+1)(D(n)+D(n+1))$ and closed-form $D(n) = n! \sum (-1)^k/k!$, concrete `native_decide` computations of $D(2)$ through $D(6)$, and two original proofs that the identity is never a derangement and that derangements do not form a subgroup of $S_n$.

title: Partial Derangements: Permutations with Exactly k Fixed Points
description: Proves S(n,k) = C(n,k)·D(n-k): the number of permutations of n elements with exactly k fixed points equals the binomial coefficient C(n,k) times the derangement number D(n-k). Verified for n=3,4,5 via native_decide. Proved via bijection between {σ | support = S} and derangements of S.

title: Partial Derangements for Arbitrary Finite Types
description: Generalizes the partial derangement formula S(n,k) = C(n,k)·D(n-k) from Fin n to arbitrary Fintype α. For any finite type α with decidable equality and k ≤ |α|, the number of permutations with exactly k fixed points equals C(|α|,k)·D(|α|-k). Proved via transport from Fin |α| using Fintype.equivFin and permutation conjugation.

title: Derangements Convergence Rate to 1/e
description: Proves the sharp convergence rate |D(n)/n! - 1/e| ≤ 1/(n+1)! using the alternating series estimation theorem. The ratio D(n)/n! equals the n-th partial sum of the Taylor series for e^{-1}, and the error is bounded by the first omitted term. Also proves D(n)/n! → 1/e and the alternating property: even partial sums overshoot 1/e from above, odd partial sums undershoot from below.

title: Second-Order Derangement Convergence Rate
description: Refines the derangement convergence rate to a two-term asymptotic: D(n)/n! = 1/e + (-1)^n/(n+1)! + O(1/(n+2)!). Proves the second-order bound, a matching lower bound showing tightness, the error ratio formula, and sign characterization of the correction term.

title: Desargues's Theorem
description: Desargues's Theorem (Wiedijk's #87): If two triangles are in perspective from a point, then they are in perspective from a line, and conversely.

title: Desargues Over Any Ring: Algebraic Proof Without Sorries
description: Can the full algebraic proof of Desargues's theorem be completed without sorries using Mathlib's linear algebra? YES — and it generalizes to any commutative ring K. This formalization defines a custom cross product (since Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.CrossProduct was deprecated in v4.26.0), proves the Lagrange cross product identity over K, and establishes Desargues's theorem in full generality: the forward direction over any CommRing K, the converse over any IntegralDomain K, and corollaries for ℚ, ℤ, 𝔽_p, and polynomial rings.

title: Non-Desarguesian Planes: The Moulton Plane Counterexample
description: How can we formalize non-Desarguesian planes in Lean to demonstrate when Desargues's theorem fails? YES — by constructing the Moulton plane, an affine plane where lines with negative slope bend at the y-axis, and exhibiting a concrete 6-point counterexample. Two triangles are perspective from a point O but their three side-intersection points are NOT Moulton-collinear, proving Desargues fails.

title: Self-Duality of Desargues's Theorem
description: Formalizes the self-duality of Desargues's theorem in projective geometry over arbitrary commutative rings. Shows that collinearity and concurrence are the same predicate in homogeneous coordinates (rfl), that the dual configuration's perspective-from-a-point equals the original's perspective-from-a-line (rfl), and that the Desargues identity is symmetric in the two triangles. Includes algebraic converse over integral domains.

title: Descartes' Rule of Signs
description: The number of positive real roots of a polynomial is either equal to the number of sign changes in the coefficient sequence, or less than it by an even number.

title: Descartes' Rule of Signs: Parity Result and Exact Count (Open Question)
description: Descartes' Rule of Signs (1637) states that the number of positive real roots of a polynomial (counted with multiplicity) is at most the number of sign variations in the coefficient sequence, and differs from it by an even number. The upper bound is now in Mathlib as `roots_countP_pos_le_signVariations`. The parity result — that the difference is always even — requires the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra plus analysis of complex conjugate pairs, and is not yet formalized in Mathlib.

title: Descartes Parity via Complex Root Theory
description: Explores proving Descartes' parity result using complex conjugate root pairs. Proves the conjugate root theorem, non-real root pairing, and parity of real root counts. Shows the factoring approach is more direct for Lean.

title: Minimal Infrastructure for Descartes Parity
description: Analyzes the minimal infrastructure needed for Descartes' parity result (signVariations ≡ positive roots mod 2). Proves that complex conjugate pairing alone is NOT sufficient — the exact sign variation change under root extraction is also required. Formalizes parity arithmetic, root decomposition, the gap analysis, and the key axiomatized lemma.

title: Budan's Theorem: Generalization of Descartes' Rule to Intervals
description: Budan's theorem (1807) generalizes Descartes' Rule of Signs from counting positive roots to counting roots in any half-open interval (a, b]. For a polynomial p of degree n, the Budan-Fourier sequence at x is [p(x), p'(x), ..., p^(n)(x)]. The sign variation count V_p(x) gives: #roots in (a,b] ≤ V_p(a) - V_p(b), with the difference being even. This is the foundation of modern polynomial root isolation algorithms.

title: Proving Budan's Upper Bound in Lean
description: Proof scaffold for the Budan upper bound theorem: the number of roots of a polynomial p in (a,b] is at most V_p(a) - V_p(b), where V_p is the Budan-Fourier sign variation count.

title: Descartes Rule OQ-03: Constructive Root Bounds and Localization
description: Combines Descartes' Rule of Signs (via Mathlib's signVariations) with the Cauchy bound (via cauchyBound) to prove constructive root localization: all roots lie in (-cauchyBound, cauchyBound), sign-variation-free polynomials have no positive roots, and Lagrange's alternative bound for tighter intervals. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

title: Descartes' Rule of Signs: Algebraic Proof via Polynomial Division (Grabiner)
description: A purely algebraic proof of Descartes' Rule of Signs following Grabiner (1999), using polynomial factoring and induction on positive root count instead of Rolle's theorem. The key insight: multiplying by (x - r) with r > 0 adds at least one sign variation to the coefficient sequence, enabling a clean induction without calculus.

title: Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions
description: For any two positive coprime integers a and q, there are infinitely many primes congruent to a modulo q. This foundational result in analytic number theory uses Dirichlet characters and L-functions.

title: Siegel Zeros: Can L(1, χ) Be Very Small? (Open Question)
description: Can L(1, χ) be extremely close to zero for real Dirichlet characters χ of large conductor? Dirichlet's theorem (in Mathlib) proves L(1, χ) ≠ 0, but how small can it get? A 'Siegel zero' would be a real zero β of L(s, χ) in (1 - c/log(q), 1) — their existence is a major open question in analytic number theory, intimately connected to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

title: Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4)
description: An elementary proof that there are infinitely many primes congruent to 3 modulo 4. This special case of Dirichlet's theorem is proved using a variant of Euclid's argument without L-functions: given any finite set of such primes, N = 4·(n+1)! - 1 ≡ 3 (mod 4) and any prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4) of N must be larger than n.

title: Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions
description: The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) asserts that all non-trivial zeros of Dirichlet L-functions L(s, χ) lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. We formalize GRH, prove equivalences between formulations, and axiomatize its dramatic consequences: improved PNT for arithmetic progressions (error O(√x log x)), effective Linnik bound (least prime O(q² log² q)), elimination of Siegel zeros, and effective class number bounds.

title: Best Constant in Linnik's Theorem for Primes in Arithmetic Progressions
description: Formalizes the Linnik constant L: the best exponent such that the least prime p ≡ a (mod q) satisfies p ≤ c·q^L. Current best: L ≤ 5 (Xylouris 2011). Conjectured: L = 1.

title: Dissection of Cubes
description: Wiedijk 100 theorem #82: a cube cannot be dissected into a finite number of smaller cubes all of different sizes. Proved by Littlewood (1953) via infinite descent — the smallest cube on any horizontal floor is surrounded by taller cubes, so its top face becomes a new floor with smaller cubes, generating an infinitely long strictly decreasing chain that contradicts finiteness. Contrasts with 2D, where perfect squared squares DO exist (Brooks-Smith-Stone-Tutte, 1940). Formalized in 366 lines with 2 axioms capturing the 3D geometric covering argument.

title: Minimum Collision Number in Cube Dissections
description: Every cube dissection must have ≥ 2 cubes sharing the same size (strengthening Wiedijk #82). This formalization proves the quantitative lower bound: the set of 'colliding cubes' in any nonempty dissection has cardinality ≥ 2. The open question is whether exactly 2 is achievable — whether a cube can be dissected with only one repeated size, all others distinct.

title: Minimal Collision is Achievable in Cube Dissections
description: Proves that HasMinimalCollision is achievable: there exists a CubeDissection with exactly 2 colliding cubes. This shows the lower bound of 2 (from OQ-01) is tight within the formalization. Three axis-aligned cubes — two of size 1/4 and one of size 1/3 — form the explicit witness, with the two equal-size cubes as the unique collision pair.

title: 3D Shape Dissection: Dehn Invariant and Hilbert's Third Problem
description: Formalizes the Dehn invariant approach to Hilbert's Third Problem: proves the cube has zero Dehn invariant (rational angles) while the tetrahedron has nonzero invariant (irrational angle), showing they cannot be scissors congruent.

title: Dehn-Sydler Completeness: Tensor Product Dehn Invariant
description: Formalizes the proper algebraic Dehn invariant D(P) ∈ ℝ ⊗_ℤ (ℝ/πℤ) using Mathlib's tensor product infrastructure. Proves rational angle vanishing (edges with rational×π dihedral angles contribute 0), cube D=0, tetrahedron D≠0, and Hilbert's Third Problem. States the Dehn-Sydler completeness theorem.

title: Cube Dissection and Packing: Connections to Impossibility
description: Explores connections between cube dissection impossibility (Wiedijk #82) and packing problems. Formalizes cube packings (disjoint containment without full coverage), proves dissection-packing bridge (impossible dissection → no perfect packing with distinct sizes), volume bounds, and the 2D vs 3D dimension contrast (squared squares exist, cubed cubes don't). 17 theorems, 0 axioms, 2 sorries.

title: Divisibility by 3 Rule
description: A natural number is divisible by 3 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. This ancient divisibility test works because 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3).

title: Formal Divisibility Rules for Various Bases and Moduli
description: A comprehensive collection of formally verified divisibility rules: general last-k-digits framework, power-of-2/5 generalizations, truncation methods for 7, 11, 13, 17, and 19, casting out nines/threes, digital root theory, and coprime factorization rules.

title: Base-b Divisibility Rules
description: Generalizes divisibility rules to arbitrary bases: for b ≥ 3, (b-1) | n iff (b-1) | digit_sum_b(n). Covers hexadecimal (mod 15), octal (mod 7), factor tests, and cross-base divisibility. All 15 theorems fully verified.

title: Efficient Digital Root Computation via Modular Arithmetic
description: Formalizes the O(1) digital root formula: digitalRoot(n) = 1 + ((n-1) mod 9) for n > 0. Proves idempotency, divisibility characterizations by 3 and 9, congruence with mod 9, and concrete examples. The closed-form formula avoids iterative digit summation.

title: Casting Out Nines: Practical Arithmetic Verification
description: Formalizes casting out nines and its generalizations: digit sums respect addition and multiplication mod 9 (and mod d for any d with b % d = 1), enabling error detection in arithmetic. All 17 theorems fully verified with 0 axioms.

title: Detection Probability for Casting Out Methods
description: Formalizes the detection probability of casting-out arithmetic checks: casting out with modulus d detects exactly (d-1)/d of all single-digit errors. Proves the core counting result (d-1 of d perturbation magnitudes are detected) both generally and for specific bases. All 22 theorems fully verified with 0 axioms.

title: General Truncation Divisibility Rule
description: A parametric theorem generalizing the truncation method to all divisors coprime to 10. Given any d coprime to 10 and an osculator c (satisfying d | 10c ∓ 1), we prove d | n ↔ d | (n/10 ± c·(n%10)). This single theorem subsumes the specific rules for 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37, and all other primes coprime to 10.

title: Unified Osculator Theorem
description: Merges the positive and negative osculator theorems into a single unified theorem with a signed osculator c in Z. The negative osculator case is derived as a corollary by substituting -c, and a dual osculator relationship theorem shows that the sum of positive and negative osculators is divisible by d.

title: Transcendence of e
description: The number e = 2.71828... is transcendental: it is not a root of any polynomial with integer coefficients. The first number proven transcendental by Hermite.

title: Is e + π Transcendental? (Open Question)
description: Is the number e + π = 5.8598... transcendental? Despite both e (Hermite, 1873) and π (Lindemann, 1882) being individually transcendental, the transcendence of their sum remains one of the most tantalizing open problems in mathematics. We prove what IS known: at least one of e+π or e·π must be transcendental — a clean consequence of e's transcendence via the Vieta symmetric polynomial identity.

title: Irrationality Measure of e
description: The irrationality measure of Euler's number e is exactly 2, the smallest possible value for any irrational number. This follows from the regular continued fraction expansion e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, ...].

title: Elementary Proof of Quadratic Reciprocity
description: Eisenstein's elegant 1844 proof of quadratic reciprocity via Gauss's Lemma, floor function sums, and lattice point counting - using only elementary arithmetic.

title: Zolotarev's Permutation-Based Proof of Quadratic Reciprocity
description: Zolotarev's 1872 proof of quadratic reciprocity via permutation signatures — the Legendre symbol (a/p) equals the sign of the multiplication-by-a permutation on (ZMod p)ˣ.

title: Gauss Sum Proof Architecture for Quadratic Reciprocity
description: Formalizes the logical skeleton of the Gauss sum proof of Quadratic Reciprocity, axiomatizing the deep cyclotomic evaluation τ² = χ(−1)·p. Demonstrates that QR follows once τ² is established, providing a third independent QR proof pathway in Lean 4 alongside the Eisenstein and Zolotarev approaches. Includes QR verification for small primes. 7 theorems, 1 axiom.

title: Jacobi Symbol and QR for Composite Moduli
description: Extends quadratic reciprocity from the Legendre symbol (prime moduli) to the Jacobi symbol (composite odd moduli), formalizing the generalized reciprocity law J(m,n)·J(n,m) = (-1)^((m-1)/2·(n-1)/2) for coprime odd m,n.

title: Jacobi Symbol: Complete Multiplicativity Structure
description: Formalizes the full multiplicative structure of the Jacobi symbol: top and bottom multiplicativity, periodicity, power laws, coprimality characterization, special reciprocity simplifications, and Euclidean reduction steps for efficient computation.

title: The Kronecker Symbol: Extending Jacobi to All Integer Moduli
description: Formalizes the Kronecker symbol χ(a,n) extending the Jacobi symbol to all integer moduli, including n=0, n=-1, n=2, and composite even n.

title: Certified Jacobi Symbol Computation via Euclidean Reduction
description: Demonstrates that the verified Euclidean reduction steps (periodicity, multiplicativity, reciprocity, supplements) can be assembled into a certified computation function for the Jacobi symbol in Lean 4.

title: The Kronecker Symbol: Extending Jacobi to All Integers
description: Defines the Kronecker symbol extending the Jacobi symbol to even moduli, negative integers, and zero. Proves values at special arguments, agreement with Jacobi for odd positive moduli, and states multiplicativity and generalized quadratic reciprocity.

title: Multiplicativity of the Kronecker Symbol (Both Arguments)
description: Proves that the Kronecker symbol is completely multiplicative in both arguments: (ab/n) = (a/n)(b/n) for ab != 0, and (a/mn) = (a/m)(a/n) for mn != 0. Uses case analysis with kronecker0 and kroneckerNeg1 multiplicativity for special moduli, and Jacobi symbol multiplicativity (jacobiSym.mul_left and jacobiSym.mul_right) for the general case.

title: Jacobi Symbol and Hilbert Symbols: The Local-Global Connection
description: Survey of how the Jacobi symbol connects to Hilbert symbols and the local-global principle. Proves Legendre-QR connections from Mathlib, axiomatizes Hilbert symbol and product formula pending p-adic infrastructure.

title: Erdős Problem #1: Distinct Subset Sums
description: If A is a subset of {1,...,N} with n elements and all 2^n subset sums are distinct, then N >> 2^n. Erdős's 'first serious problem' (1931). OPEN with $500 prize.

title: Dubroff–Fox–Xu Subset Sum Lower Bound Framework
description: Formalizes the algebraic framework for the Dubroff–Fox–Xu (2021) lower bound N ≥ √(2/π) · 2ⁿ/√n for the distinct subset sums problem (Erdős #1). Proves variance bounds (sum of squares ≤ n·N², sum ≤ n·N) and axiomatizes the anticoncentration step from Berry–Esseen.

title: Conway-Guy Construction for Distinct Subset Sums
description: Formalizes the Conway-Guy sequence (OEIS A005318) for Erdos Problem #1. Defines the sequence, verifies initial values and recurrence relation, proves structural properties (exceeds half-sum, counting bound, strict monotonicity, growth rate), and states the optimality conjecture.

title: Sums of a Prime and Powers of 2
description: Is there some k such that every sufficiently large integer is the sum of a prime and at most k powers of 2? Erdős and Graham conjectured no such k exists. Gallagher showed the representable set has density arbitrarily close to 1.

title: Finite k for Sufficiently Large Integers (Erdős #10 OQ-01)
description: Does there exist a finite k such that every sufficiently large integer is the sum of a prime and at most k powers of 2? Formalizes the logical hierarchy from Gallagher's density theorem through Crocker's impossibility to the Erdős-Graham conjecture. Shows that the Granville-Soundararajan conjecture would imply k=4 suffices for all n ≥ 3.

title: Erdős #100: Point Sets with Restricted Distances
description: Let A be n points in ℝ² with all pairwise distances ≥ 1 and any two distinct distances differing by ≥ 1. Must the diameter be ≫ n? Known: n^(3/4) (Kanold), n/log n (Guth-Katz). Piepmeyer: 9 points with diameter < 5.

title: Distance Set Diameter: Linear vs Logarithmic Growth Gap
description: Analyzes the gap between the known diameter bound Ω(n/log n) from Guth–Katz and the conjectured linear bound Ω(n) for integer distance sets. Proves the gap factor log n grows without bound, n/log n = o(n), and the linear conjecture implies the known bound. States the Anning–Erdős finiteness constraint.

title: Erdős #100 OQ: Distance Set Diameter Growth Rate
description: Is the minimum diameter of n-point integer distance sets Θ(n) (linear) or Θ(n/log n)?

title: Erdős #1000: Generalized Totients and Diophantine Approximation
description: For an infinite sequence A = {n₁ < n₂ < ...}, define φ_A(k) as the count of m ≤ n_k such that m/n_k in lowest form has denominator different from all previous n_j. Does lim (1/N) Σ φ_A(k)/n_k = 0 for some A? Answer: YES (Haight), contrary to Erdős' expectation.

title: Erdős #1001: Diophantine Approximation Density
description: Let S(N,A,c) measure α ∈ (0,1) with |α - x/y| < A/y² for some N ≤ y ≤ cN, gcd(x,y)=1. Does lim S(N,A,c) exist? YES (Kesten-Sós). Formula: f(A,c) = 12A log(c)/π² in EST regime.

title: Erdős #1001 OQ: Rate of Convergence of S(N,A,c)
description: What is the rate at which S(N,A,c) approaches f(A,c)? In the EST regime (0 < A < c/(1+c²)) where approximation intervals are disjoint, the rate is O(A log N / N). This formalization axiomatizes this rate, reduces it to the error in weighted Euler totient sums, and derives consequences including that convergence is faster than O(1/√N).

title: Erdős #1001 OQ-03: Higher-Dimensional Diophantine Approximation Density
description: Higher-dimensional generalization of the Erdős #1001 Diophantine approximation density problem. For α ∈ [0,1]^d, the measure of vectors approximable by primitive rationals p/q (N ≤ q ≤ cN) with max|α_i - p_i/q| < A/q^{1+1/d} converges to f_d(A,c) = (2A)^d·log(c)/ζ(d+1). For d=1: recovers the EST formula 12A·log(c)/π². The proof uses Jordan's d-th totient function and a d-dimensional Mertens theorem.

title: Erdős Problem #1002: Asymptotic Distribution of Weighted Fractional Sums
description: For 0 < α < 1, define f(α,n) = (1/log n) Σ (1/2 - {αk}). Does f(α,n) have an asymptotic distribution function? Kesten (1960) proved the two-parameter variant has Cauchy distribution, but the one-parameter case remains open.

title: Erdős #1002 OQ-01: Proving Cauchy CDF and Periodic Sum Axioms
description: Eliminates two axioms from the Erdős #1002 formalization: proves the Cauchy CDF is a valid distribution function (monotone, correct limits) and proves periodicity of the inner sum for rational arguments.

title: Erdős Problem #1003: Consecutive Equal Totients
description: Are there infinitely many solutions to φ(n) = φ(n+1), where φ is the Euler totient function? Erdős conjectured yes, and made the stronger claim that φ(n) = φ(n+1) = ... = φ(n+k) has infinitely many solutions for every k ≥ 1.

title: Erdős #1004: Distinct Consecutive Totient Values
description: For c > 0, if x is large, does there exist n ≤ x such that φ(n+1), ..., φ(n+⌊(log x)^c⌋) are all distinct? EPS (1987) proved K ≤ n/exp(c(log n)^{1/3}).

title: Erdős Problem #1005: Farey Fractions and Similar Ordering
description: Let f(n) be the longest run of consecutive similarly ordered Farey fractions of order n. Estimate f(n) - is there c > 0 with f(n) = (c + o(1))n? Known: (1/12 - o(1))n ≤ f(n) ≤ n/4 + O(1).

title: Erdős Problem #1006: Robust Acyclic Orientations
description: Can every graph with girth > 4 be oriented so that there is no directed cycle, and reversing any single edge also creates no directed cycle? Disproved by Nešetřil-Rödl (1978) for all girths.

title: Robustly Acyclic Orientations and Cover Graphs
description: Formalizes Erdős Problem #1006 (OQ-01): characterize which graphs admit robustly acyclic orientations. Axiomatizes the Pretzel-Brightwell characterization (1985): a graph admits a robustly acyclic orientation iff it is a cover graph of some poset. Also axiomatizes: Nešetřil-Rödl counterexamples (1978) for all girths, Fisher-Fraughnaugh-Langley-West criterion (χ < girth implies robust). Proves empty and bipartite graphs have robust orientations. 6 theorems, 3 axioms.

title: Minimum Chromatic Number for Non-Robustly-Orientable Graphs
description: For a graph with girth g that admits no robustly acyclic orientation, what is the minimum possible chromatic number? The answer is exactly g: Fisher-Fraughnaugh-Langley-West (1997) proved χ(G) < girth(G) implies robust orientability, establishing the lower bound χ ≥ g. The Grötzsch graph (girth 4, χ=4) witnesses tightness at g=4.

title: Direct Proof: FFLLW Chromatic Number Bound via Coloring Orientations
description: A direct Lean 4 proof of the Fisher-Fraughnaugh-Langley-West (FFLLW) theorem from Mathlib primitives: if χ(G) < girth(G), then G admits a robustly acyclic orientation. The proof constructs the coloring orientation (orient u→v when col(u) < col(v)) and shows it is always robustly acyclic. Key insight: under the rank-based formulation, ANY properly colorable finite graph has a robust orientation, making the girth condition unnecessary.

title: Erdős Problem #1007: Graph Dimension
description: What is the smallest number of edges in a graph with dimension 4? The answer is 9, achieved uniquely by K_{3,3}. Graph dimension is the minimum Euclidean dimension for unit-distance embedding.

title: Minimum Edges for Graph Dimension d
description: Studies the function minEdges(d) giving the minimum number of edges in a graph of dimension exactly d. Formalizes known values (d=0..5), proves structural results including a constructive simplex embedding of K_n in ℝⁿ, shows the complete graph optimality conjecture implies monotonicity, analyzes growth rates, and introduces the deficiency function.

title: Is minEdges Monotone in d?
description: Investigates whether the function minEdges(d) — the minimum number of edges in a graph of dimension exactly d — is monotone (non-decreasing). Proves monotonicity for known values (d ≤ 5), establishes that the full conjecture reduces to consecutive monotonicity for d ≥ 5, and proves the key structural result that a deficiency bound δ(d) ≤ d implies monotonicity.

title: Graph Dimension: Axiom Elimination Analysis
description: Analysis of axioms in the Erdős #1007 (graph dimension) formalization. Proves hasUnitEmbedding_exists via scaled basis vectors (4→3 axioms). The remaining axioms (min_edges_dimension_4/5, k33_unique_minimum) are deep results from House 2013 and Chaffee-Noble 2016.

title: Erdős Problem #1008: C₄-Free Subgraphs
description: Does every graph with m edges contain a C₄-free subgraph with ≫ m^{2/3} edges? Yes, proved by Conlon-Fox-Sudakov (2014). The exponent 2/3 is optimal, as shown by Folkman's counterexample K_{n,n²}.

title: Optimal Constants in the C₄-Free Subgraph Bound
description: What are the optimal constants in the Ω(m^{2/3}) bound for C₄-free subgraphs? Formalizes the framework for the optimal constant question, proves the K_{2,2}=C₄ equivalence, and establishes structural properties of C₄-free graphs.

title: Erdős Problem #1009: Edge-Disjoint Triangles Beyond Turán
description: For every c > 0, does there exist f(c) such that every graph with ⌊n²/4⌋ + k edges (k < cn) contains at least k - f(c) edge-disjoint triangles? SOLVED: Györi (1988) proved this with f(c) ≪ c².

title: Edge-Disjoint K₄ Copies Beyond Turán
description: Is there a K₄ analogue of Györi's theorem? If a graph on n vertices has more than ex(n, K₄) = ⌊n²/3⌋ edges (the Turán threshold for K₄-free graphs), can we guarantee many edge-disjoint K₄ copies?

title: Erdős Problem #101: Four-Point Lines from Planar Point Sets
description: Given n points in ℝ² with no five collinear, is the number of lines containing exactly four points o(n²)? Grünbaum: ≫ n^{3/2}. Solymosi–Stojaković: n^{2−O(1/√log n)}. Open.

title: Erdős Problem #1010: Triangle Supersaturation
description: For t < ⌊n/2⌋, every graph on n vertices with ⌊n²/4⌋ + t edges contains at least t·⌊n/2⌋ triangles. This quantifies the supersaturation phenomenon: how many triangles are forced when exceeding the Turán threshold.

title: Erdős #1010 OQ2: Supersaturation for K_r
description: Generalize triangle supersaturation to K_r: what is the minimum number of r-cliques in a graph exceeding the Turán threshold ex(n, K_r)? Solved for r=3 (Razborov 2010) and r=4 (Reiher 2016), open for r≥5.

title: Erdős Problem #1011: Triangles in Graphs with High Chromatic Number
description: Let f_r(n) be minimal such that every n-vertex graph with ≥ f_r(n) edges and χ ≥ r contains a triangle. Known: f_2(n) = ⌊n²/4⌋+1 (Turán), f_3(n) = ⌊(n-1)²/4⌋+2 (Erdős-Gallai). Asymptotic involves g(r) ~ r² log r. OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1012: Long Cycles in Dense Graphs
description: Let f(k) be such that every graph on n ≥ f(k) vertices with ≥ C(n-k-1,2) + C(k+2,2) + 1 edges has an (n-k)-cycle. Woodall (1972) proved f(k) ≤ 2k+3 and such graphs are pancyclic from 3 to n-k.

title: Erdős #1012 OQ-01: Exact Value of f(k) for Long Cycles
description: Formalizes the exact characterization of f(k): the minimum n₀ such that dense enough graphs contain an (n-k)-cycle. Proves f(0)=f(1)=1 (Ore 1961, Bondy 1971), f(k)=2k+3 for k≥2 (Woodall 1972). Axiomatizes Ore's Hamiltonian cycle theorem, Bondy's pancyclicity theorem, Woodall's cycle theorem, and the tight lower bound construction. Proves growth rate analysis and threshold symmetry. 37 theorems, 5 definitions, 4 axioms.

title: Erdős #1012 OQ-02: Vertex-Pancyclicity in Dense Graphs
description: Strengthens Woodall's pancyclicity result to vertex-pancyclicity: every vertex lies on cycles of all lengths 3 to n-k, not just that the graph contains such cycles. Formalizes Bondy's vertex-pancyclicity theorem (1971: dense Hamiltonian graphs are vertex-pancyclic or bipartite), Schmeichel-Hakimi (1988: Ore-type vertex-pancyclicity), and Woodall's vertex-pancyclic extension. 12 theorems, 5 definitions, 2 axioms.

title: Directed Graph Hamiltonian Cycle Thresholds
description: Directed analogues of Hamiltonian cycle conditions: Ghouila-Houri, Moon-Moser, and Rédei theorems for digraphs and tournaments.

title: Triangle-Free Chromatic Threshold
description: Let h_3(k) be the smallest n with a triangle-free graph on n vertices of chromatic number k. Find the asymptotic formula. Known: (1/2 - o(1))k^2 log k <= h_3(k) <= (1 + o(1))k^2 log k. Is h_3(k+1)/h_3(k) -> 1?

title: Erdős Problem #1014: Ramsey Number Ratio Convergence
description: For fixed k ≥ 3, prove that R(k, l+1)/R(k, l) → 1 as l → ∞, where R(k, l) is the Ramsey number. Open even for k = 3. Status: OPEN.

title: Erdős #1014 (k=3): Ramsey Ratio Convergence from Recurrence
description: Proves R(3,l+1)/R(3,l) → 1 as l → ∞ using only the Ramsey recurrence R(3,l+1) ≤ R(3,l) + R(2,l+1), the trivial value R(2,l) = l, and the Kim-Shearer lower bound R(3,l) ≥ c·l²/log l. The key insight is that the recurrence constrains consecutive increments to O(l), while the quadratic-over-log lower bound shows the values themselves grow much faster.

title: Erdős #1014 OQ-02: Rate of Convergence is O(log l / l)
description: Answers the open question: what is the rate of convergence of R(k,l+1)/R(k,l) to 1? For k=3, the rate is O(log l / l), which is strictly faster than O(1/log l). The proof combines the Ramsey recurrence bound R(3,l+1) - R(3,l) ≤ l+1 with the Kim lower bound R(3,l) ≥ c·l²/log l. Also proves that log l/l < 1/log l for large l. For general k, the ratio converges to 1 under conjectured asymptotics (proved via ratio_from_asymptotics).

title: Erdős Problem #1015: Partitioning 2-Colored Complete Graphs
description: What is f(t), the minimum leftover vertices when partitioning any 2-colored Kₙ into vertex-disjoint monochromatic Kₜ's? Burr-Erdős-Spencer (1975) proved f(t) = R(t, t-1) + x where 0 ≤ x < t, showing f(t)^{1/t} → 4 (not 1) and f(t) is not O(t).

title: Erdős #1015 OQ1: Exact Values of f(t) for Small t ≥ 4
description: Computes bounds on f(t) — the minimum leftover in monochromatic clique partitions of 2-colored complete graphs — for t = 4 and t = 5 via the Burr-Erdős-Spencer formula. Shows f(4) ∈ {9,10,11,12}, f(5) ∈ {25,...,29}, proves f(t) grows exponentially, and answers Erdős's questions: f(t)^{1/t} → 4 ≠ 1 and f(t) ≠ O(t).

title: Erdős #1015 OQ5: Axiom Elimination via Erdős-Szekeres Bound
description: Investigates which of the 8 axioms in the Erdős #1015 formalization can be proved from Mathlib. Eliminates 2: replaces the axiomatized ramseyNumber with a proper definition via Nat.find, and proves R(t,t) ≤ 4^t via the Erdős-Szekeres bound R(r,s) ≤ C(r+s-2, r-1).

title: Pancyclic Excess Edges
description: Let h(n) be the minimum excess edges beyond n for an n-vertex pancyclic graph (containing all cycle lengths 3 to n). Estimate h(n): is h(n) >= log_2 n + log* n - O(1)? Known: log_2(n-1) - 1 <= h(n) <= log_2 n + log* n + O(1).

title: Erdős Problem #1017: Clique Partition of Graphs
description: Let f(n,k) be the min cliques to partition any graph with n vertices, k edges. Erdős-Goodman-Pósa proved f(n,k) ≤ n²/4. Can this be improved for k > n²/4? The K₄-free case is solved (Győri-Keszegh 2017).

title: Clique Partition of Dense Graphs: Can K₄ Improve the EGP Bound?
description: Can f(n,k) < ⌊n²/4⌋ when k > n²/4? Formalizes the Erdős-Goodman-Pósa framework, tightness via K_{n/2,n/2}, and the Győri-Keszegh K₄-free resolution. The general case with K₄ and larger cliques remains open.

title: Erdős Problem #1018: Non-Planar Subgraphs in Dense Graphs
description: For ε > 0, does every graph with n vertices and n^(1+ε) edges contain a non-planar subgraph on O_ε(1) vertices? Kostochka-Pyber (1988) proved yes: such graphs contain K₅ subdivisions on constantly many vertices.

title: Hypergraph Extension of Non-Planar Subgraph Density
description: Extends Erdős 1018 (Kostochka-Pyber) to r-uniform hypergraphs: does n^(r-1+ε) edge density force a non-embeddable sub-hypergraph on O_{r,ε}(1) vertices? Uses the van Kampen-Flores theorem (K_{2r+1}^(r) is not embeddable in R^(2(r-1))) as the topological obstruction.

title: Hypergraph Non-Planar Density: Concrete Embeddability Definition
description: Completion pass for Erdős #1018 OQ-04. Replaces the sorry `isEmbeddable` definition with a concrete topological definition via vertex maps and convex hull separation. Provides explicit planar coordinates for K₃ and K₄, proves K₅ has 10 edges, and connects dense graphs to non-embeddable subgraphs via Kostochka-Pyber (r=2 case axiomatized).

title: Erdős Problem #1019: Saturated Planar Subgraphs in Dense Graphs
description: Does every graph on n vertices with ⌊n²/4⌋ + ⌊(n+1)/2⌋ edges contain a saturated planar graph with more than 3 vertices? Simonovits proved yes: such graphs must contain K₄ or C_l + 2K₁.

title: Erdős Problem #102: Maximum Collinear Points Forced by Many Rich Lines
description: Given n points with cn² lines containing ≥ 4 points, estimate h_c(n) = max collinear. Known: ≤ C√n. Erdős's √n lower conjecture disproved by Hunter. Open.

title: Erdős Problem #1020: The Erdős Matching Conjecture
description: Let f(n;r,k) be max edges in r-uniform hypergraph with no k independent edges. Conjecture: f(n;r,k) = max(C(rk-1,r), C(n,r)-C(n-k+1,r)). Solved for r=2,3. Upper bound: (k-1)C(n-1,r-1). OPEN for r≥4.

title: Erdős Problem #1021: Extremal Numbers for Bipartite Pair Graphs
description: For k ≥ 3, does there exist c_k > 0 such that ex(n, G_k) ≪ n^(3/2 - c_k)? Here G_k is the bipartite graph with k primary vertices and C(k,2) pair vertices. Even ex(n, G_k) = o(n^(3/2)) is unknown.

title: Extremal Numbers for G_k: Does ex(n, G_k) = o(n^{3/2}) for k ≥ 4?
description: Focuses on the weak form of Erdős Problem #1021 for k ≥ 4: does ex(n, G_k) = o(n^{3/2})? The k=3 case is settled (Bondy-Simonovits, ex(n,C_6) ≪ n^{7/6}). Formalizes the trivial KST upper bound, the probabilistic lower bound, and the gap between O(n^{3/2}) and o(n^{3/2}).

title: Erdős Problem #1022: Property B and Sparse Set Families
description: Is there c_t → ∞ such that if F is a family of sets of size ≥ t, and for every X there are < c_t|X| subsets of X in F, then F has property B (2-colorable)? Known: c_2 = 1 (Lovász 1968).

title: Property B_k: k-Colorability of Hypergraphs
description: Generalizes Property B (2-colorability) to Property B_k (k-colorability). Proves monotonicity in k, equivalence B ↔ B_2, and states the generalized first-moment threshold k^{t-1}/(k-1).

title: Erdős Problem #1023: Union-Free Families
description: Let F(n) be the max size of a family of subsets of {1,...,n} where no set is the union of other members. Is F(n) ~ c · 2^n / √n? YES: F(n) = C(n, n/2) ~ √(2/π) · 2^n / √n.

title: Erdős #1023 OQ-01: k-Union-Free Families
description: Extends Erdős Problem #1023 (union-free families) to k-union-free families. Proves F(n) = C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) using the Erdős-Kleitman result. Formalizes k-union-free generalization, antichain structure, symmetric-difference-free families, and Stirling approximation for the central binomial constant √(2/π). Verifies small cases computationally. 36 theorems, 20 definitions, 2 axioms.

title: Erdős Problem #1024: Independent Sets in Linear Hypergraphs
description: Let f(n) be the minimum independence number guaranteed in every 3-uniform linear hypergraph on n vertices. Phelps-Rödl (1986) proved f(n) ≍ (n log n)^(1/2), refining Erdős's bounds n^(1/2) ≪ f(n) ≪ n^(2/3).

title: Erdős Problem #1025: Independent Sets in Pair Functions
description: Let f map pairs from {1,...,n} to {1,...,n} with f(x,y) ≠ x,y. Let g(n) be the minimum guaranteed independent set size. Erdős-Hajnal (1958) proved n^(1/3) ≪ g(n) ≪ (n log n)^(1/2). Spencer (1972) and Conlon-Fox-Sudakov (2016) determined g(n) = Θ(n^(1/2)).

title: Erdős Problem #1026: Monotonic Subsequence Sum Optimization
description: For a sequence of distinct reals, determine max sum over monotonic subsequences. The optimal constant is c = 1: maxMonotonicSum ≥ (1-o(1)) · totalSum/√n. This is a weighted Erdős-Szekeres theorem.

title: Erdős Problem #1027: Intersecting Sets and Property B
description: Let F be a family of at most c·2^n sets of size n, and X = ∪F. Must there exist ≫_c 2^|X| sets B ⊆ X that intersect every set in F yet contain none? YES (proved by Koishi Chan). Connection to Property B (2-chromatic families).

title: Erdős Problem #1028: Discrepancy of Sign Functions
description: Let H(n) = min_f max_X |∑_{x≠y∈X} f(x,y)| where f: pairs → {±1}. Erdős (1963) proved n/4 ≤ H(n) ≪ n^(3/2). Erdős-Spencer (1971) proved H(n) ≫ n^(3/2). Answer: H(n) = Θ(n^(3/2)).

title: Erdős Problem #1029: Ramsey Number Growth Rate
description: If R(k) is the diagonal Ramsey number, prove R(k)/(k·2^{k/2}) → ∞. Known bounds: (√2/e)·k·2^{k/2} ≤ R(k) ≤ C(2k-2,k-1). OPEN ($100 proof, $1000 disproof).

title: Erdős Problem #103: Incongruent Optimal Point Configurations
description: Let h(n) count the number of incongruent sets of n points in ℝ² that minimize diameter with d(x,y) ≥ 1 for all distinct x,y. Is h(n) → ∞?

title: Erdos #103 OQ-01: Does h(n) tend to infinity?
description: Investigation of whether h(n), the count of incongruent optimal point configurations with minimum separation 1 and minimal diameter, tends to infinity. Proves isometry injectivity, constructs isometry inverses, eliminates congruent_symm sorry, and demonstrates that the parent file's 'unbounded iff tends to infinity' equivalence is logically false without monotonicity.

title: Erdős Problem #1030: Ramsey Number Growth Rate
description: Prove the existence of c > 0 such that lim_{k→∞} R(k+1,k)/R(k,k) > 1+c. Solved by Burr-Erdős-Faudree-Schelp (1989) who proved R(k+1,k) - R(k,k) ≥ 2k-5.

title: Erdős Problem #1031: Induced Regular Subgraphs in Non-Ramsey Graphs
description: If G on n vertices has no trivial subgraph on ≥ 10 log n vertices, must G contain an induced non-trivial regular subgraph on ≫ log n vertices? YES (Prömel-Rödl 1999). Stronger: such G is c log n - universal.

title: Erdős Problem #1032: 4-Chromatic Critical Graphs with High Minimum Degree
description: Do there exist 4-chromatic critical graphs on n vertices with minimum degree linear in n? Dirac achieved δ > n/2 for k=6; Simonovits–Toft achieved δ ≫ n^{1/3} for k=4.

title: Erdős Problem #1033: Triangle Degree Sums in Dense Graphs
description: Let h(n) = max k such that every graph on n vertices with > n²/4 edges contains a triangle with degree sum ≥ k. Conjecture: h(n) ≥ (2(√3−1)−o(1))n ≈ 1.464n. Known: (21/16)n ≤ h(n) ≤ 2(√3−1)n.

title: Erdős Problem #1034: Triangle Neighbors in Dense Graphs
description: Let G have n vertices and > n²/4 edges. Must there exist a triangle T with > (1/2 - o(1))n vertices each adjacent to ≥ 2 of T's vertices? NO (Ma-Tang). Bounds: (1/6)n ≤ h(n) ≤ (2 - √(5/2))n ≈ 0.419n.

title: Hypercube Subgraphs in Dense Graphs
description: Is there c > 0 such that every graph on 2^n vertices with min degree > (1-c)·2^n contains the hypercube Q_n? Related to extremal graph theory for hypercube embeddings.

title: Erdős Problem #1036: Distinct Induced Subgraphs in Non-Ramsey Graphs
description: Let G be non-Ramsey (no trivial subgraph on > c log n vertices). Must G contain ≥ 2^{Ω_c(n)} non-isomorphic induced subgraphs? YES (Shelah 1998). Prior: Alon-Hajnal (1991) proved exp(n(log n)^{-O(log log n)}).

title: Erdős Problem #1037: Degree Diversity and Ramsey Properties
description: Let G have n vertices where every degree occurs at most twice and distinct degrees > (1/2 + ε)n. Must G have a trivial subgraph much larger than log n? NO (Cambie-Chan-Hunter). Counterexample: ≥ 3n/4 distinct degrees, max trivial O(log n).

title: Erdős Problem #1038: Sublevel Sets of Monic Polynomials
description: Determine the infimum and supremum of the measure of {x : |f(x)| < 1} for monic polynomials with roots in [-1,1]. Supremum = 2√2 (Tao, 2025); infimum bounds: 1.519 ≤ inf ≤ 1.835.

title: Erdős Problem #1039: Polynomial Lemniscate Disc Radius
description: Let f(z) = ∏(z-zᵢ) with |zᵢ| ≤ 1. Let ρ(f) = radius of largest disc in {z: |f(z)| < 1}. Is ρ(f) ≫ 1/n? OPEN. Known: 1/(2en²) ≤ ρ(f) (Pommerenke), ρ(f) ≫ 1/(n√log n) (KLR 2025). Upper: ρ(zⁿ-1) ≤ π/(2n).

title: Erdős Problem #104: Unit Circles Through Three Points
description: Given n points in ℝ², how many unit circles contain at least 3 points? Known: Ω(n^{3/2}) ≤ answer ≤ O(n²). Conjecture: O(n^{3/2}). OPEN ($100 prize).

title: Erdős Problem #1040: Transfinite Diameter and Sublevel Set Measure
description: Let F ⊆ ℂ be closed infinite, μ(F) = inf of |{z: |f(z)| < 1}| over polynomials with roots in F. Is μ(F) determined by transfinite diameter? Is μ(F) = 0 when ρ(F) ≥ 1? OPEN. Known for line segments/discs (EHP 1958).

title: Erdős Problem #1041: Paths in Polynomial Level Sets
description: For a monic polynomial with all roots in the unit disk, must there exist a path of length less than 2 in the sublevel set {z : |f(z)| < 1} connecting two roots?

title: Erdős Problem #1042: Connected Components of Polynomial Lemniscates
description: For polynomials with roots in a closed set F ⊆ ℂ, how many connected components can the lemniscate {z : |f(z)| < 1} have? Depends on transfinite diameter and geometry. SOLVED by Ghosh-Ramachandran (2024).

title: Erdős #1043: Polynomial Level Set Projections
description: For a monic polynomial f, must some line's projection of {z : |f(z)| ≤ 1} have measure ≤ 2? NO (Pommerenke 1961): can be ≥ 2.386, but always ≤ 3.3.

title: Erdős Problem #1044: Boundary Length of Polynomial Level Sets
description: For polynomials f(z) with all roots in the unit disk, what is the infimum of the maximum boundary length of connected components of {z : |f(z)| < 1}? Tang proved the answer is 2, achieved in the limit but not by any specific polynomial.

title: Erdős Problem #1045: Maximum Product of Distances
description: Given n complex points with pairwise distances ≤ 2, maximize ∏|zᵢ-zⱼ|. Regular polygon is NOT optimal for even n ≥ 4. Odd n case remains open.

title: Lemniscate Containment in a Disc
description: For monic f ∈ ℂ[x], if E = {z : |f(z)| < 1} is connected, is E in a disc of radius 2? YES (Pommerenke 1959). The center is the root centroid. But the width conjecture is FALSE.

title: Erdős Problem #1047: Convexity of Polynomial Lemniscates
description: Must the connected components of {z : |f(z)| ≤ c} be convex for small c? No! Grunsky's conjecture was disproved by Pommerenke (1961) and Goodman (1966) with explicit counterexamples.

title: Erdős Problem #1048: Polynomial Lemniscate Diameter
description: For a monic polynomial f ∈ ℂ[x] with roots in |z| ≤ r where r < 2, must L(f,1) = {z : |f(z)| < 1} have a component with diameter > 2-r? DISPROVED by Pommerenke (1961) for r > 1.

title: Erdős Problem #1049: Irrationality of Divisor Sums
description: For rational t > 1, is ∑_{n≥1} 1/(t^n - 1) = ∑_{n≥1} τ(n)/t^n irrational? OPEN: Erdős proved YES for integer t ≥ 2. Chowla's conjecture for all rationals unresolved.

title: Erdős Problem #105: Lines Avoiding a Point Set
description: Given n points A (not collinear) and n-3 points B, must some line hit 2+ points of A and miss B entirely? DISPROVED by Xichuan with explicit counterexamples. Variants with n-4 or (1-o(1))n remain open.

title: Erdos #105 OQ-05: Rich Flats in Higher Dimensions
description: Higher-dimensional generalization of Erdos #105: does the rich-line vs obstacle phenomenon extend to k-flats in R^d? We formalize lines and 2-flats in R^d, prove rich lines exist trivially, establish monotonicity properties, and state the open conjectures.

title: Erdős Problem #1050: Irrationality of ∑ 1/(2^n - 3)
description: Is ∑_{n≥1} 1/(2^n - 3) irrational? SOLVED by Borwein (1991): YES. More generally, ∑ 1/(q^n + r) is irrational for q ≥ 2 and rational r ≠ 0, r ≠ -q^n.

title: Erdős Problem #1051: Irrationality of Reciprocal Product Series
description: If a₁ < a₂ < ⋯ are integers with lim inf aₙ^{1/2ⁿ} > 1, is Σ 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) irrational? Known for rapid growth aₙ₊₁ ≥ C·aₙ². OPEN in general.

title: Erdős #1052: Unitary Perfect Numbers
description: A unitary perfect number equals the sum of its proper unitary divisors (where d is unitary if gcd(d, n/d)=1). All unitary perfect numbers are even; finiteness is OPEN. Three examples verified by native_decide.

title: Erdős Problem #1053: Growth Rate of k-Perfect Numbers
description: If σ(n) = k·n (n is k-perfect), must k = o(log log n)? Known: k ≤ 11 exists. Gronwall: σ(n)/n = O(log log n). Robin's inequality gives k = O(log log n) conditionally on RH. Status: OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1054: Sum of Smallest Divisors
description: Let f(n) be the minimal integer m such that n equals the sum of the k smallest divisors of m for some k ≥ 1. Is f(n) = o(n)? Or is this true only for almost all n, with limsup f(n)/n = ∞?

title: Erdős #1054: f(n) = o(n) for Almost All n
description: Erdős asked whether the function f(n) — the minimal m whose partial divisor sums include n — satisfies f(n) = o(n) for almost all n. Tao disproved the unconditional form, but the 'almost all' version remains open. We formalize the density framework and prove accessible bounds via the sigma bound f(σ(m)) ≤ m, showing the ratio m/σ(m) → 0 along superabundant numbers.

title: Erdős Problem #1055: Prime Classification by p+1 Factorization
description: Classify primes by the factorization depth of p+1. Class 1: p+1 is 3-smooth. Class r: all prime factors of p+1 have class ≤ r-1. Are there infinitely many primes in each class? How does p_r^{1/r} grow? Status: OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1056: Consecutive Interval Products ≡ 1 (mod p)
description: For k ≥ 2, does there exist a prime p and k consecutive intervals whose products are all ≡ 1 (mod p)? Known for k=2 (p=11, Erdős 1979) and k=3 (p=17, Makowski 1983). Guy's Problem A15. Status: OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1057: Counting Carmichael Numbers
description: Let C(x) count Carmichael numbers in [1,x]. Is C(x) = x^{1-o(1)}? Known: x^{0.3389} < C(x) < x·exp(-c·log x·log log log x / log log x). OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1058: Prime Divisors of n!+1 Between Consecutive Primes
description: Are there only finitely many n in [p_{k-1}, p_k) such that the only primes dividing n!+1 are p_k and p_{k+1}? SOLVED: Luca (2001) proved the only solutions are n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

title: Erdős Problem #1059: Primes Minus Factorials All Composite
description: Are there infinitely many primes p such that p - k! is composite for every k with 1 ≤ k! < p? Examples include p = 101 and p = 211. The heuristic suggests most large primes satisfy this property. Status: OPEN.

title: Selberg Sieve Framework for Erdős Problem 1059
description: Formalizes the Selberg sieve framework for proving Erdős Problem #1059 (infinitely many primes p with all p - k! composite). Introduces primorial intervals I(l) = (l!, (l+1)!], proves structural lemmas, and shows the Selberg density estimate implies the conjecture. The key analytic bound is axiomatized.

title: Smallest Prime > 211 Failing Erdős 1059
description: The smallest prime p > 211 failing the Erdős 1059 property (all p - k! composite) is p = 223. Since 223 - 4! = 199 is prime, 223 does not satisfy the property. Fully verified by decision procedure with 0 sorries and 0 axioms.

title: Decidable Factorial Compositeness Verification
description: A Decidable instance for AllFactorialSubtractionsComposite eliminates the need for manual per-prime factorial bound helpers. Any concrete prime can now be verified with a single native_decide.

title: Erdős Problem #106: Square Packing in the Unit Square
description: Pack n squares in the unit square with disjoint interiors. Let f(n) = max sum of side lengths. Is f(k²+1) = k? Known: f(k²) = k, f(2) = 1, f(5) = 2. Axis-parallel case solved (2024). OPEN.

title: Can Rotated Squares Beat Axis-Parallel Packings?
description: Formalizes the open question of whether rotated squares can achieve a strictly larger total side-length sum than axis-parallel arrangements when packing squares in the unit square. Defines RotatedSquare with angle parameter, general vs axis-parallel packings, proves agreement at perfect squares, and states the open question f_rot(n) > g(n). Related to Erdős Problem #106 and the BKU axis-parallel breakthrough (2024).

title: Erdős Problem #1060: Counting Solutions to k·σ(k) = n
description: Let f(n) count solutions to k·σ(k) = n. Is f(n) ≤ n^{o(1/log log n)}? Perhaps even f(n) ≤ (log n)^{O(1)}? This problem remains OPEN.

title: Erdos Problem #1061: Additive Divisor Equation
description: How many ordered pairs (a,b) satisfy sigma(a)+sigma(b)=sigma(a+b) with a+b<=x? Is this count asymptotic to cx for some c>0?

title: Erdős Problem #1062: Maximum "No Divides Two Others" Sets
description: Let f(n) = max |A| for A ⊆ {1,…,n} with no element dividing two distinct others. Lebensold: 0.6725n ≤ f(n) ≤ 0.6736n. Is lim f(n)/n irrational? OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1063: Binomial Coefficient Divisibility
description: Let k >= 2. Find the least n_k >= 2k where all but one of {n,...,n-k+1} divide C(n,k). Known: n_2=4, n_3=6, n_4=9, n_5=12. Upper bounds: n_k <= k! (Monier). OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1064: Comparing φ(n) and φ(n - φ(n))
description: Is φ(n) > φ(n - φ(n)) for almost all n? Yes (density 1), but the reverse holds infinitely often. Solved by Luca-Pomerance and Grytczuk-Luca-Wójtowicz.

title: Erdős Problem #1065: Primes of the Form 2^k · q + 1
description: Erdős Problem #1065 (Guy's B46): Are there infinitely many primes $p = 2^k \cdot q + 1$ with $q$ prime and $k \geq 0$? More generally, $p = 2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q + 1$? Connected to safe primes ($k=1$) and smooth-minus-one primes. The formalization axiomatizes both conjecture variants, verifies all 15 Form A primes ≤ 100, proves strict inclusion Form A ⊊ Form B with formal non-examples, and includes structural theorems. 301 lines, 0 sorries, 2 axioms. OEIS A074781, A339465.

title: Bateman-Horn Density for Primes p = 2^k · q + 1
description: Formalization of Bateman-Horn density predictions for Erdős #1065 Form A primes. Defines IsFormAWithK parameterized by k, proves safe primes ↔ k=1, states uniqueness of the (k,q) decomposition, verifies k-value distribution for all 15 Form A primes ≤ 100, and axiomatizes the BH conjecture that each k-layer is infinite with constant 2C₂ independent of k.

title: Erdős Problem #1066: Independence Number of Unit Distance Graphs
description: Let G be a graph given by n points in ℝ² where any two distinct points are at least distance 1 apart, and we draw an edge between two points if they are distance exactly 1 apart. Let g(n) be maximal such that any such graph always has an independent set on at least g(n) vertices. Estimate g(n), or perhaps lim g(n)/n.

title: Higher-Dimensional Unit Distance Independence
description: Explores g_d(n) — the independence number of unit distance graphs in ℝ^d. The kissing number τ(d) bounds vertex degrees, giving g_d(n) ≥ n/(τ(d)+1) by greedy coloring. Known kissing numbers (τ(8)=240, τ(24)=196560) are encoded; the greedy bound is axiomatized. Includes exact values for d=1,2,3 and the scaling behavior as d→∞.

title: Erdős Problem #1067: Infinitely Connected Subgraphs with Chromatic Number ℵ₁
description: Does every graph with χ = ℵ₁ contain an infinitely connected subgraph with χ = ℵ₁? DISPROVED by Soukup (2015), Bowler-Pitz (2024).

title: Erdős Problem #1068: Countable Infinitely-Connected Subgraphs
description: Does every graph with chromatic number ℵ₁ contain a countable infinitely vertex-connected subgraph? Soukup (2015): uncountable sets can fail. Version of Erdős–Hajnal problem. Open.

title: Erdős Problem #1069: Szemerédi-Trotter Theorem on k-Rich Lines
description: Given n points in ℝ², the number of k-rich lines (containing ≥k points) is O(n²/k³) for k ≤ √n. Proved by Szemerédi-Trotter (1983).

title: Erdos Problem #107: The Happy Ending Problem
description: Let f(n) be minimal such that any f(n) points in R^2, no three collinear, contain n points forming a convex n-gon. The conjecture f(n) = 2^{n-2} + 1 remains OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1070: Independence Number of Unit Distance Graphs
description: Estimate f(n), the minimum independence number of n-point unit distance graphs in ℝ². Is f(n) ≥ n/4? Best bounds: 0.22936n ≤ f(n) ≤ (2/7)n. The n/4 question cannot be resolved via density methods.

title: Maximal Packings of Unit Segments in the Unit Square
description: Can finitely many non-intersecting unit segments in [0,1]² be maximal? Yes (Danzer). Can a countably infinite maximal packing exist in some region? Open.

title: Erdős Problem #1072: Least n with n! ≡ −1 (mod p)
description: For prime p, let f(p) be the least n with n! + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p). By Wilson's theorem, f(p) ≤ p-1. Are there infinitely many p with f(p) = p-1? Is f(p)/p → 0 for almost all p? Status: OPEN.

title: Composites Dividing Factorial Plus One
description: Let A(x) count composites u < x with u | n!+1 for some n. Is A(x) ≤ x^{o(1)}? Wilson's theorem covers primes. Known composites: 25, 121, 169, 437, ...

title: Erdős Problem #1074: EHS Numbers and Pillai Primes
description: Do the asymptotic densities of EHS numbers and Pillai primes exist? Both sets are infinite (Erdős-Hardy-Subbarao), but density questions remain OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1075: Dense Subgraphs in r-Uniform Hypergraphs
description: For r ≥ 3, does there exist c_r > r^{-r} such that any r-uniform hypergraph on n vertices with ≥ (1+ε)(n/r)^r edges contains an m-vertex subgraph with ≥ c_r·m^r edges? Erdős proved c_r = r^{-r} works with threshold εn^r. Status: OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1076: Extremal Numbers for 3-Uniform Hypergraphs
description: For k ≥ 5, let F_k be all 3-uniform hypergraphs with k vertices and k-2 edges. Is ex₃(n, F_k) ~ n²/6? SOLVED: YES (Bohman-Warnke 2019, Glock-Kühn-Lo-Osthus 2020).

title: Erdős Problem #1077: Balanced Subgraphs in Dense Graphs
description: Must dense graphs contain large balanced subgraphs? Jiang-Longbrake (2025) showed the optimal size is Θ(n^α) vertices, resolving ambiguities in the original problem.

title: Erdős Problem #1078: Minimum Degree for K_r in r-Partite Graphs
description: In r-partite graphs with n vertices per part, min degree ≥ (r-3/2-o(1))n implies K_r exists. SOLVED by Haxell (2001). Sharp threshold by Haxell-Szabó (2006).

title: Erdős Problem #1079: Turán Density in Neighborhoods
description: For r ≥ 4, if G has n vertices and at least ex(n; K_r) edges, must G contain a vertex whose neighborhood is also Turán-dense? YES, proved by Bollobás–Thomason (1981) and strengthened by Bondy (1983).

title: Erdős Problem #108: High Chromatic Subgraphs with Large Girth
description: For every r >= 4 and k >= 2, does there exist f(k,r) such that every graph with chromatic number >= f(k,r) contains a subgraph of girth >= r and chromatic number >= k?

title: Erdős Problem #1080: Six-Cycles in Sparse Bipartite Graphs
description: Is there a constant c > 0 such that bipartite graphs with n vertices (one part of size ⌊n^(2/3)⌋) and cn edges must contain a C_6? NO, disproved by De Caen-Székely (1992).

title: Erdős Problem #1081: Sums of Two Squarefull Numbers
description: Let A(x) count integers n ≤ x that are sums of two squarefull numbers. Is A(x) ~ c·x/√(log x)? NO, disproved by Odoni (1981). Correct asymptotic: A(x) ~ x/(log x)^α where α = 1-2^(-1/3) ≈ 0.206.

title: Erdős Problem #1082: Distinct Distances in General Position
description: Let A ⊂ ℝ² be n points with no three collinear. Does A determine ≥ n/2 distinct distances? The stronger form (single point with n/2 distances) was disproved by Xichuan.

title: Erdős Problem #1083: Distinct Distances in Higher Dimensions
description: Let d ≥ 3, and let f_d(n) be the minimal m such that every n-point set in ℝ^d determines at least m distinct distances. Is f_d(n) = n^{2/d - o(1)}?

title: Erdős Problem #1084: Unit Distances Among Separated Points
description: Let f_d(n) be the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in ℝ^d with all pairwise distances ≥ 1. For d=2, Harborth gave the exact formula. For d=3, Erdős conjectured f_3(n) = 6n - Θ(n^{2/3}). Status: OPEN (d ≥ 3).

title: Erdos #1084 OQ-01: f_3(n) = 6n - Theta(n^{2/3})
description: Is f_3(n) = 6n - Theta(n^{2/3})? Formalization of the Erdos conjecture on the correction term for unit-distance pairs among separated points in 3D, with proved kissing-number upper bounds and isoperimetric exponent analysis.

title: Erdős Problem #1085: The Unit Distance Problem
description: Let f_d(n) be the maximum number of pairs at unit distance among n points in ℝ^d. For d=2: n^(1+o(1)) ≤ f_2(n) ≤ O(n^(4/3)) with gap OPEN. For d≥4: f_d(n) ≈ (p-1)/(2p)·n² where p=⌊d/2⌋ (essentially SOLVED).

title: Erdős Problem #1086: Triangles of Equal Area
description: Let g(n) be the maximum number of triangles with the same area determined by n points in ℝ². Best bounds: n² log log n ≪ g(n) ≪ n^{20/9} (Erdős-Purdy 1971, Raz-Sharir 2017). The Erdős-Purdy conjecture predicts g(n) = Θ(n² polylog(n)). Higher-dimensional generalizations involve g_d^r(n) for r-simplices in ℝ^d. Status: OPEN.

title: Erdos Problem #1087: Degenerate Quadruples in Point Sets
description: Estimate f(n), the maximum number of degenerate 4-point sets in n points in the plane. Is f(n) at most n^{3+o(1)}?

title: Erdős Problem #1088: Distinct Distance Subsets in High Dimensions
description: Let f_d(n) be the minimal m such that any m points in ℝ^d contain n points with all pairwise distances distinct. Is f_d(n) = 2^{o(d)} for fixed n ≥ 3? OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1089: Distinct Distances in Higher Dimensions
description: Let g_d(n) be minimal such that every g_d(n) points in ℝ^d determine at least n distinct distances. Does lim_{d→∞} g_d(n)/d^{n-1} exist? Known: g_d(n) ≫ d^{n-1}, but g_d(n) ≤ c^{d^{1-b_n}}. OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #109: The Sumset Conjecture
description: Any subset A of natural numbers with positive upper density contains a sumset B + C where both B and C are infinite.

title: Erdős Problem #1090: Monochromatic Collinear Points
description: For k ≥ 3, does there exist a finite set A ⊂ ℝ² such that any 2-coloring has k monochromatic collinear points? SOLVED: YES. Graham-Selfridge proved k=3; Hunter used Hales-Jewett for general k.

title: Erdos Problem #1091: Odd Cycles with Diagonals in K4-Free Graphs
description: Must a K4-free graph with chi(G) = 4 contain an odd cycle with at least two diagonals? Answer: YES (Voss 1982). General f(r) question: OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1092: Chromatic Decomposition Threshold
description: Let f_r(n) be max edges removable from each subgraph to reduce chromatic number to ≤ r while forcing χ(G) ≤ r+1. Is f₂(n) ≫ n? Rödl (1982) gives f₂(n) = O(n·polylog). Open.

title: Erdős Problem #1093: Deficiency of Binomial Coefficients
description: For n ≥ 2k with C(n,k) having no prime factor ≤ k, the deficiency counts k-smooth terms among n, n-1, ..., n-k+1. Are there infinitely many with deficiency 1? Only finitely many with deficiency > 1? OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1094: Least Prime Factor of Binomial Coefficients
description: For n ≥ 2k, the least prime factor of C(n,k) should be ≤ max(n/k, k) with only finitely many exceptions. OPEN.

title: Erdős Problem #1095: The Erdős-Selfridge Function
description: Let g(k) be the smallest n > k+1 such that all prime factors of C(n,k) exceed k. Estimate g(k). Known: exp(c·(log k)²) ≪ g(k) ≤ exp((1+o(1))k). Conjectured: log g(k) ~ k/log k. OPEN.

title: Erdős #1095 OQ01: Asymptotics of g(k) — Smooth Binomial Coefficients
description: Is log g(k) ~ c·k/log k, where g(k) is the smallest n > k+1 with all prime factors of C(n,k) exceeding k?

title: Erdős Problem #1096: Gap Convergence in q-Expansions
description: For 1 < q < 1 + ε, do gaps in the sequence of q-representable numbers tend to 0? Conjectured threshold: smallest Pisot number q₀ ≈ 1.3247.

title: Common Differences in Three-Term Arithmetic Progressions
